claims.text: A conventional tempered martensitic steel, such as a low-alloy high-carbon steel, can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Properly tuned tempering induces impurity segregation at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation momentarily embrittles the steel within a narrow intermediate-temperature window.
An as-quenched martensitic steel with sufficient impurity content is a suitable initial material state.
Tempering around 400–500 °C promotes impurity segregation in the proposed steel.
Phosphorus, tin, arsenic, or antimony can accumulate at grain boundaries during tempering.
At low temperatures, limited impurity diffusion preserves ductility.
In an intermediate-temperature regime, enhanced impurity diffusivity causes grain-boundary segregation.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation reduces boundary cohesion and causes embrittlement.
At higher temperatures, further diffusion or healing effects restore ductile behavior.
The steel will display a measurable intermediate-temperature dip in ductility or fracture toughness.
The steel will be ductile at lower temperatures because impurity mobility is insufficient.
The steel will be ductile at higher temperatures because segregation is mitigated.
High-entropy or compositionally complex alloys do not exhibit temper embrittlement and remain consistently ductile across the tested temperature range.
The transition occurs only in conventional alloys having sufficient impurity content and microstructures that permit grain-boundary segregation.
Alloys with suppressed diffusivity or high multi-element complexity are not expected to exhibit this transition.
The transition temperature and magnitude depend on alloy chemistry, impurity level, and heat-treatment parameters.

contradictions.description: The intervention first tempers the samples at an intermediate temperature and then tests them across temperatures, but the mechanism attributes segregation and its reversal directly to impurity mobility at the mechanical-test temperature. Segregation already produced during tempering would not necessarily disappear merely because a tempered specimen is subsequently tested at a lower temperature, so heat-treatment temperature and test temperature are internally conflated.

The hypothesis describes embrittlement as being induced by tempering within a narrow temperature window, whereas the predicted outcome describes a reversible ductility dip across the mechanical-testing temperature ramp. These are distinct temperature-dependent phenomena unless separate heat treatments are applied at each temperature.
